messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Javier Alvarez was a 62-year-old Latin American man who had spent most of his adult life as a dancer, a profession that made his body both his livelihood and, after the collision, a source of uncertainty. He described himself as a married man who had always relied on movement, rhythm, and routine, and he was struck by how violently that ordinary order had been interrupted one evening when he was driving home after work. Another vehicle hit his car in a way he experienced as unmistakably life-threatening; in the moments after impact, everything seemed to break into fragments of sound and sensation. He recalled the crash less as a sequence of events than as a rush of terror, with noises and bodily impressions taking over before his mind could make sense of what had happened. Even later, when he tried to tell the story, he found that he could not put the frightening event into words. It stayed with him as a wordless, bodily knowing rather than a clear narrative.

In the weeks that followed, Javier began to notice that memories of the collision did not arrive like ordinary recollections. At times, when something brought the crash to mind, he would suddenly hear the same sounds that had pierced him during the event, as though the screeching, impact, and surrounding noise were replaying inside his head. Those moments left him flooded with shame, not only because the memory itself felt humiliating and exposed, but because he had come to believe that the accident said something about the sort of person he was. He would think, with a kind of harsh certainty, that the event happened to him because of who he was, as if the collision had confirmed some personal flaw or weakness. He also found himself convinced that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again. This belief was especially painful for someone whose work and identity had long depended on expressive feeling; he described an eerie sense that what had once come naturally to him now felt distant or inaccessible.

As the months went on, Javier tried in several ways to keep the experience at bay. He deliberately tried to leave his body or blank out when thoughts of the crash pressed in, and he made a habit of staying up until very late so that he would not have to face the night and the possibility of being alone with his mind. He also tried hard not to think about the trauma at all, pushing away anything that might bring it into view. These efforts gave him brief relief, but they also left him living in a narrow, watchful state. He became intensely alert to signs of danger and entered rooms by immediately scanning for exits, as though he needed to know how to get out before anything could happen. In public places he noticed himself doing this almost automatically, checking doorways and routes without fully deciding to. He was also startled when someone touched him unexpectedly. A hand on his shoulder, a brush in a crowded space, or even a casual approach from behind could make him react with alarm before he had time to identify who it was.

At work, these reactions were difficult to hide. As a dancer, Javier spent time in studios, theaters, rehearsal rooms, and backstage areas where people moved close to one another and physical contact was often part of the environment. Unexpected touch from colleagues or being surprised by someone entering suddenly from behind could leave him visibly tense. He found himself orienting quickly toward doors and exits when he arrived at a rehearsal hall, and this habit made him feel less present in the work he once experienced as fluid and embodied. At home, his wife noticed that he often remained awake long after she had gone to bed, and his late nights became part of the lonely rhythm of his effort to keep the memory from rising.

By the time he sought help, Javier was troubled by how much of his life had become organized around these attempts to stay distant from the crash and alert to its return. He was exhausted by the shame that came with remembering, frightened by how sharply sounds could return in his mind, and disturbed by the sense that his own reactions to the world had become unreliable. What finally brought him in was the combination of his sleeplessness, his growing unease in crowded or touch-filled settings, and the fear that he was becoming less and less able to inhabit his own life. He hoped, more than anything, that treatment might help him feel safe enough to sleep at night and to move through his work and marriage without feeling that danger was waiting in every room.
